_link.title: I can explain how light intensity, temperature, wind and humidity affect the rate of transpiration

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the rate of transpiration when light intensity increases?

options.text: The rate increases because stomata open wider for greater CO₂ entry
The rate decreases because light causes stomata to close
The rate stays the same because light does not affect stomata
The rate decreases because light heats the cuticle, sealing pores

explanations.a: Correct. Light causes stomata to open wider for greater entry of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, which also allows greater evaporation of water.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Light causes stomata to open wider, not close. Increased light increases the transpiration rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Light does affect stomata. It stimulates them to open wider, increasing transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Light does not seal pores. It causes stomata to open, increasing the rate of transpiration.

toLevel2.stem: How does an increase in temperature affect transpiration?

options.text: Transpiration rate increases because molecules have more kinetic energy, speeding up evaporation
Transpiration rate decreases because heat closes the stomata
Transpiration rate stays the same because temperature only affects roots
Transpiration rate decreases because hot air holds less water vapour

explanations.a: Correct. As temperature increases, so does the kinetic energy of molecules, which means osmosis and evaporation occur faster, increasing transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Higher temperature increases evaporation rate. While extreme heat can cause stomatal closure, the general effect of rising temperature is increased transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Temperature affects the whole plant, including evaporation at leaf surfaces, not just the roots.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Hot air can actually hold more water vapour than cool air. Higher temperatures increase the rate of evaporation.

toLevel2.stem: What effect does wind have on the rate of transpiration?

options.text: Wind increases transpiration by removing water vapour from around stomata
Wind decreases transpiration by cooling the leaf surface
Wind has no effect on transpiration rate
Wind decreases transpiration by pushing stomata shut

explanations.a: Correct. In windy conditions, water vapour is removed more quickly from around stomata, keeping the concentration gradient high and increasing the rate of evaporation.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While wind may cool leaves slightly, its main effect is removing water vapour, which increases transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Wind does affect transpiration by maintaining a steep concentration gradient around the stomata.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Wind does not push stomata shut. Guard cells control stomatal opening and closing through osmosis.

toLevel2.stem: How does high humidity affect the rate of transpiration?

options.text: Transpiration rate decreases because the concentration gradient between the leaf and the air is reduced
Transpiration rate increases because moist air enters stomata
Transpiration rate increases because humidity opens stomata wider
Transpiration rate stays the same because humidity only affects roots

explanations.a: Correct. When the air is humid, there is more water vapour present. Humid air is less able to accept water molecules by evaporation, reducing the concentration gradient and slowing transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Moist air does not enter stomata to increase transpiration. High humidity reduces the driving force for evaporation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Humidity does not directly cause stomata to open wider. It reduces the concentration gradient, slowing transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Humidity affects the air surrounding the leaves and directly impacts the rate of evaporation through stomata.

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following conditions would result in the highest rate of transpiration?

options.text: Bright light, warm temperature, windy, low humidity
Low light, cool temperature, still air, high humidity
Bright light, cool temperature, still air, high humidity
Low light, warm temperature, windy, low humidity

explanations.a: Correct. High light intensity opens stomata wider, warm temperatures increase kinetic energy, wind removes water vapour, and low humidity maintains a steep concentration gradient — all maximise transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Low light, cool temperatures, still air, and high humidity all reduce the rate of transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Although bright light promotes stomatal opening, cool temperatures, still air, and high humidity would counteract this and reduce transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Low light means stomata are less open, which limits transpiration even though the other conditions are favourable.

toLevel2.stem: Windy conditions increase the rate of transpiration by removing water vapour from around stomata.

options.text: True
False

explanations.a: Correct. Wind removes water vapour from around stomata, maintaining a high concentration gradient between the leaf and the air, which increases the rate of transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Wind does increase transpiration. It removes water vapour from the leaf surface, keeping the concentration gradient steep and promoting faster evaporation.

toLevel2.stem: High humidity increases the rate of transpiration because moist air absorbs more water.

options.text: True
False

explanations.a: Incorrect. High humidity decreases transpiration because humid air already contains a lot of water vapour, reducing the concentration gradient needed for evaporation.
explanations.b: Correct. High humidity decreases transpiration. When the air is already saturated with water vapour, the concentration gradient between the leaf and the air is reduced, slowing evaporation.

toLevel2.stem: As temperature increases, the {{blank:1}} of molecules increases, which speeds up evaporation.
Wind increases transpiration by keeping the {{blank:1}} between the leaf and the air high.
Light causes stomata to open wider for greater entry of {{blank:1}} for photosynthesis.

toLevel3.stem: Why does wind increase the rate of transpiration even though it does not directly affect stomata?

options.text: Wind removes the layer of humid air around stomata, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for water vapour to diffuse out
Wind pushes water molecules back into the leaf through the stomata
Wind forces stomata open by exerting physical pressure on guard cells
Wind brings carbon dioxide to the leaf, which forces water out of stomata

explanations.a: Correct. Wind removes the water vapour that accumulates around the leaf surface, maintaining a high concentration gradient that drives faster evaporation from stomata.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Wind removes water vapour from the leaf surface; it does not push water back into the leaf.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Wind does not physically open stomata. Guard cells control stomatal opening through changes in turgor pressure.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While air movement may bring CO₂, this is not why wind increases transpiration. The key effect is removing water vapour.

toLevel3.stem: Explain why increased temperature causes faster transpiration.

options.text: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, so they evaporate from cell surfaces and diffuse through stomata faster
Higher temperature causes the cuticle to melt, allowing water to escape from all leaf surfaces
Higher temperature makes the xylem expand, pushing water out through the leaves
Higher temperature causes roots to absorb water faster, which forces it out through leaves

explanations.a: Correct. Increased temperature raises the kinetic energy of water molecules, causing them to evaporate faster from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffuse more rapidly through stomata.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The waxy cuticle does not melt at normal environmental temperatures. Water loss primarily occurs through stomata.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Xylem does not expand significantly with temperature. The increase in transpiration is due to faster evaporation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While root absorption may increase slightly, the main cause of faster transpiration is increased evaporation rate at the leaf surfaces.

toLevel3.stem: Why does high humidity reduce the rate of transpiration?

options.text: Because the air already contains a high concentration of water vapour, reducing the concentration gradient that drives evaporation
Because humid air is heavier and physically blocks stomata
Because humidity causes guard cells to become flaccid and close stomata
Because humid air absorbs heat from the leaf, cooling it down

explanations.a: Correct. In humid conditions, the air already holds a lot of water vapour. This reduces the concentration gradient between the moist air inside the leaf and the external air, slowing evaporation.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Humid air does not physically block stomata. The effect is on the concentration gradient for water vapour.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Humidity does not directly cause guard cells to become flaccid. The reduced transpiration is due to a smaller concentration gradient.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While humid air may have different thermal properties, the main reason it reduces transpiration is the reduced concentration gradient.

toLevel3.stem: How does the relationship between light and stomata explain the effect of light on transpiration?

options.text: Light stimulates stomata to open wider for CO₂ uptake, which simultaneously increases the surface area for water vapour loss
Light heats the leaf surface, which directly evaporates water from the cuticle
Light provides energy for active transport of water out through stomata
Light breaks down the cuticle, exposing more of the leaf to air

explanations.a: Correct. Light causes stomata to open wider so more CO₂ can enter for photosynthesis. The wider opening also allows more water vapour to escape, increasing transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While light may warm leaves slightly, most water loss occurs through stomata, not the cuticle. The key mechanism is stomatal opening.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Transpiration is a passive process driven by evaporation and concentration gradients, not active transport.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Light does not break down the cuticle. The cuticle is a stable waxy layer.

toLevel3.stem: Why would a plant placed in a sealed transparent container show very little water loss?

options.text: The enclosed air becomes saturated with water vapour, reducing the concentration gradient to near zero and halting transpiration
The container blocks all light from reaching the plant
The plant cannot photosynthesise in a container, so it closes all stomata permanently
The container prevents wind from entering, and wind is the only factor that drives transpiration

explanations.a: Correct. In a sealed container, transpired water vapour cannot escape. The air quickly becomes humid, reducing the concentration gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air to near zero.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A transparent container allows light to pass through, so the plant still receives light.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The plant can still photosynthesise in a transparent container. The reduced transpiration is due to the saturated air, not a lack of photosynthesis.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Wind is not the only factor driving transpiration. The concentration gradient is the fundamental driving force, and in a sealed container it approaches zero.

toLevel3.stem: In what way does the concentration gradient explain the effect of each environmental factor on transpiration?

options.text: All four factors either steepen or flatten the water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf interior and the surrounding air
All four factors directly control guard cell turgor through osmosis
All four factors change the amount of water absorbed by the roots
All four factors affect the thickness of the cuticle on the leaf surface

explanations.a: Correct. Light, temperature, wind, and humidity all ultimately affect the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air — the driving force for transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While some factors may indirectly influence guard cells, not all four directly control guard cell turgor. Wind and humidity act on the external concentration gradient.
explanations.c: Incorrect. These factors primarily affect evaporation from leaves, not water absorption by roots.
explanations.d: Incorrect. None of these factors change the thickness of the cuticle. They affect the concentration gradient for water vapour.

toLevel3.stem: Light increases transpiration because it directly heats the water inside xylem vessels.

options.text: True
False

explanations.a: Incorrect. Light increases transpiration primarily by causing stomata to open wider for CO₂ uptake, not by directly heating xylem water.
explanations.b: Correct. The main mechanism is that light stimulates stomata to open wider for photosynthesis, which increases the area available for water vapour loss.

toLevel3.stem: Humid air is less able to accept water molecules by evaporation, which reduces the {{blank:1}} and slows transpiration.
In a sealed transparent container, transpiration nearly stops because the air becomes {{blank:1}} with water vapour.
Light increases transpiration indirectly by causing {{blank:1}} to open wider for carbon dioxide entry.

toLevel4.stem: A student sets up two identical plants: one in front of a fan and one in still air, both in the same room. After 4 hours, the plant near the fan has lost more mass. What explains this result?

options.text: The fan removed water vapour from around the leaves, maintaining a steep concentration gradient and increasing transpiration
The fan blew water directly out of the stomata
The fan caused the stomata to open wider by vibrating the guard cells
The fan cooled the leaves, which increased the rate of evaporation

explanations.a: Correct. The fan mimics wind by continuously removing the humid air layer around the leaves, keeping the concentration gradient high and driving faster transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The fan does not blow water out of stomata directly. It removes the layer of water vapour around the leaf, maintaining a concentration gradient.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Guard cells open and close through osmosis, not vibration. The fan does not physically open stomata.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Cooling the leaves would actually slow evaporation. The fan increases transpiration by removing water vapour, not by cooling.

toLevel4.stem: A gardener waters plants in the early morning rather than at midday. Which combination of factors best explains why this is beneficial?

options.text: At midday, high temperature and light cause rapid transpiration, so water is lost before roots can absorb enough to support the plant
At midday, the soil is too hot for roots to function, so water cannot be absorbed
In the morning, humidity is always at zero so water goes directly to the roots
In the morning, stomata are permanently closed so no water is lost

explanations.a: Correct. At midday, high temperature and intense light drive rapid transpiration. Watering in the cooler morning allows roots to absorb water before peak transpiration demand.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Roots can function in warm soil. The issue is that transpiration demand at midday may exceed the rate of water uptake.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Humidity is not zero in the morning. Morning watering is beneficial because transpiration rates are lower.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Stomata are not permanently closed in the morning. They open in response to light, but conditions are less extreme than at midday.

toLevel4.stem: An experiment measures transpiration rate in four conditions. In which condition would you expect the lowest rate?

options.text: Dark, cool, still air, high humidity
Bright light, warm, windy, low humidity
Bright light, warm, still air, low humidity
Dark, warm, windy, low humidity

explanations.a: Correct. Darkness keeps stomata mostly closed, cool temperature reduces kinetic energy, still air allows water vapour to accumulate, and high humidity reduces the concentration gradient — all minimising transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This combination of bright light, warmth, wind, and low humidity would produce the highest transpiration rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Bright light and warmth still drive significant transpiration even without wind.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Although darkness limits stomatal opening, warmth, wind, and low humidity still allow some transpiration.

toLevel4.stem: A student places a plastic bag over a leafy branch on a sunny day and observes water droplets forming inside the bag. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Water vapour lost through transpiration condensed inside the bag because it could not escape into the surrounding air
Rain entered the bag through small holes in the plastic
The leaves absorbed water from the air and released it as liquid
Photosynthesis produced water as a by-product that leaked out of the leaves

explanations.a: Correct. The bag trapped water vapour released through stomata during transpiration. As the air inside became saturated, the water vapour condensed into visible droplets.
explanations.b: Incorrect. If the bag is properly sealed, no rain can enter. The water comes from transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Leaves lose water through transpiration; they do not absorb it from the air in this way.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Photosynthesis produces oxygen, not water, as a by-product. The water droplets come from transpiration.

toLevel4.stem: A florist recommends keeping cut flowers in a cool room away from draughts. How does this advice relate to factors affecting transpiration?

options.text: Cool temperatures reduce evaporation rate and still air prevents the removal of water vapour, both slowing transpiration and keeping flowers hydrated longer
Cool temperatures freeze the water in the xylem, preventing any water movement
Draughts carry bacteria that block stomata and cause the flowers to wilt
Cool rooms have more oxygen, which keeps the flowers alive longer

explanations.a: Correct. Lower temperature means less kinetic energy for evaporation, and still air allows water vapour to accumulate near the leaves, reducing the concentration gradient. Both slow transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A cool room does not freeze water in xylem. It simply slows the rate of evaporation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The benefit of avoiding draughts is reducing transpiration rate, not avoiding bacteria.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Oxygen levels are not significantly different in cool rooms. The benefit is reduced transpiration.

toLevel4.stem: Rodney pruned most of the leaves from his rose bush before transplanting it. How does this help the plant survive the move?

options.text: Removing leaves reduces the number of stomata, lowering transpiration so the damaged root system is not overwhelmed by water demand
Removing leaves makes the plant lighter so it is easier to carry
Removing leaves forces the plant to photosynthesise through its roots instead
Removing leaves prevents sunlight from reaching the soil and drying it out

explanations.a: Correct. Transplanting damages roots, reducing water uptake. Pruning leaves removes stomata, reducing transpiration so water loss does not exceed the damaged root system's ability to absorb water.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While the plant may be lighter, the purpose of pruning is to reduce transpiration and prevent wilting.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Roots do not photosynthesise. The benefit of leaf removal is reducing water loss through transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Pruning is about reducing the plant's own water loss, not about soil moisture from sunlight.

toLevel4.stem: A student argues that placing a potted plant near a heater will increase transpiration. Is this correct, and why?

options.text: Yes, because the heater raises temperature, increasing kinetic energy of water molecules and the rate of evaporation from leaf surfaces
No, because heat always closes stomata so transpiration decreases
No, because the heater produces light which is the only factor that affects transpiration
Yes, because the heater provides energy for active transport of water out of stomata

explanations.a: Correct. Higher temperature from the heater increases kinetic energy, causing water molecules to evaporate more quickly from mesophyll surfaces and diffuse faster through stomata.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While extreme heat can cause stomatal closure, moderate increases in temperature generally increase evaporation and therefore transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Temperature is a separate factor from light, and both affect transpiration. A heater provides heat, not light.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Transpiration is a passive process driven by evaporation, not active transport.

toLevel4.stem: Pruning leaves before transplanting reduces the number of {{blank:1}}, which lowers the transpiration rate.
A plant in front of a fan loses more mass because the fan maintains a steep {{blank:1}} for water vapour around the leaves.
Cut flowers last longer in a cool room because lower temperature reduces the {{blank:1}} of water molecules.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher records transpiration rates for the same plant species at four locations. Analyse which location would show the highest daily transpiration.

options.text: An exposed coastal hillside with strong sun, warm winds, and low humidity
A shaded rainforest floor with still, humid air and moderate temperature
An underground cave with no light, cool temperature, and saturated air
A sealed greenhouse with bright light, warm temperature, and no ventilation

explanations.a: Correct. Strong sun opens stomata, warm temperature increases kinetic energy, wind removes water vapour, and low humidity maintains a steep concentration gradient — all maximising transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Shade limits stomatal opening, still air allows water vapour to accumulate, and high humidity reduces the concentration gradient, all reducing transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. No light means stomata are mostly closed, and saturated air eliminates the concentration gradient, effectively stopping transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While a sealed greenhouse has light and warmth, the lack of ventilation allows humidity to build up inside, eventually reducing the concentration gradient and slowing transpiration.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that temperature is the most important factor affecting transpiration because it directly increases evaporation. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: The claim overlooks that the number of open stomata is the biggest factor, and stomatal opening is mainly controlled by light, not temperature
The claim is correct because temperature is the only factor that affects the kinetic energy of water
The claim is correct because all other factors depend on temperature
The claim is wrong because temperature has no effect on transpiration

explanations.a: Correct. While temperature does increase evaporation, the textbook states that the biggest factor affecting transpiration rate is the number of open stomata. Since stomata open mainly in response to light, light is often the more critical variable.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Temperature is not the only factor affecting kinetic energy. Also, the number of open stomata is the biggest factor overall, not temperature alone.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Light, wind, and humidity act independently of temperature in many respects. They are separate environmental factors.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Temperature does affect transpiration by increasing kinetic energy and evaporation rate, but it is not the most important factor.

toLevel5.stem: Two plants of the same species are grown in identical conditions except Plant A is in still air and Plant B has a constant breeze. After a week, Plant B shows signs of water stress. Analyse the cause.

options.text: The constant breeze continuously removed water vapour from Plant B's stomata, increasing transpiration until water loss exceeded root absorption
The breeze blew nutrients away from Plant B's roots, starving it
The breeze physically damaged Plant B's leaves, blocking all stomata
Plant B received less light because the breeze moved its leaves constantly

explanations.a: Correct. A constant breeze maintains a steep concentration gradient around the stomata by removing water vapour, driving higher transpiration. Over time, water loss exceeded the roots' ability to replace it.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Wind does not blow nutrients away from roots in the soil. The water stress is caused by excessive transpiration.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A gentle breeze does not physically damage leaves or block stomata.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Leaf movement from a breeze does not significantly reduce light availability.

toLevel5.stem: A student designs an experiment testing the effect of humidity on transpiration but conducts it outdoors on different days. Evaluate the experimental design.

options.text: The design is flawed because outdoor conditions vary in temperature, light, and wind between days, making it impossible to isolate humidity as the independent variable
The design is valid because humidity is the only factor that changes between days
The design is valid because all outdoor conditions affect transpiration equally
The design is flawed because humidity cannot be measured outdoors

explanations.a: Correct. Conducting the experiment on different days means temperature, light, and wind also vary. These confounding variables make it impossible to conclude that differences in transpiration are caused solely by humidity.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Many environmental conditions change between days, not just humidity. Temperature, wind, and light intensity all vary.
explanations.c: Incorrect. All factors do affect transpiration, which is precisely why they need to be controlled to test just one variable.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Humidity can be measured outdoors using a hygrometer. The issue is controlling other variables, not measuring humidity.

toLevel5.stem: A plant is placed in a warm, well-lit room with a dehumidifier running nearby. Analyse how the dehumidifier affects transpiration compared to normal room conditions.

options.text: The dehumidifier removes water vapour from the air, steepening the concentration gradient and increasing the transpiration rate beyond normal
The dehumidifier has no effect because only wind and light affect transpiration
The dehumidifier decreases transpiration by cooling the air around the plant
The dehumidifier increases root absorption but does not change transpiration

explanations.a: Correct. By removing water vapour from the air, the dehumidifier lowers humidity. This steepens the concentration gradient between the leaf interior and the surrounding air, driving faster evaporation and higher transpiration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Humidity is one of the four key factors affecting transpiration. Reducing humidity increases the concentration gradient.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While a dehumidifier may slightly affect air temperature, its primary effect is reducing humidity, which increases transpiration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The dehumidifier affects the air around the leaves, increasing transpiration by reducing humidity.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate why a greenhouse with automatic ventilation fans would produce healthier plants than a sealed greenhouse, in terms of transpiration.

options.text: Ventilation prevents excessive humidity buildup that would reduce transpiration and impair the transpiration stream needed for mineral transport and cooling
Ventilation provides more carbon dioxide for faster photosynthesis only
Ventilation is only useful for cooling and has no effect on transpiration
Ventilation increases humidity, which makes plants grow faster

explanations.a: Correct. In a sealed greenhouse, transpired water accumulates and humidity rises, reducing the concentration gradient and slowing transpiration. Ventilation removes humid air, maintaining transpiration which is essential for mineral transport and leaf cooling.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While ventilation does help with CO₂ supply, its effect on transpiration by controlling humidity is also critical for plant health.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Ventilation affects transpiration by reducing humidity around the leaves, maintaining the concentration gradient for water vapour loss.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Ventilation reduces humidity by removing moist air, which increases (not decreases) transpiration.

toLevel5.stem: On a still, humid evening with fading light, a student measures transpiration rate and finds it is very low. Analyse which factor contributes most to this low rate.

options.text: Fading light, because it causes stomata to close, and the number of open stomata is the biggest factor affecting transpiration rate
High humidity, because it is the only factor that can slow transpiration
Still air, because wind is the only factor that drives transpiration
All three contribute equally because each factor has the same weight

explanations.a: Correct. Fading light causes stomata to close, and the number of open stomata is by far the biggest factor affecting transpiration rate. While still air and high humidity also slow transpiration, stomatal closure has the greatest impact.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Humidity does reduce transpiration, but it is not the only factor. The number of open stomata is the biggest factor overall.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Wind is not the only factor. Stomatal closure from low light has a greater effect than still air alone.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The factors do not have equal weight. The number of open stomata is the dominant factor.

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'Since all four factors affect transpiration, changing any one of them will always produce a measurable change in water loss.' Evaluate this statement.

options.text: The statement is oversimplified because if stomata are closed due to darkness, changes in wind, temperature, or humidity have minimal effect since there is little surface area for evaporation
The statement is correct because each factor independently controls transpiration regardless of other conditions
The statement is correct because all four factors are equally important at all times
The statement is wrong because only light affects transpiration

explanations.a: Correct. The factors interact. If stomata are closed (e.g. in darkness), changes in wind, temperature, or humidity have little effect because there is minimal surface area for water vapour to escape through.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The factors do not act in complete isolation. For example, wind has little effect if stomata are already closed.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The factors are not equally important. The number of open stomata is the biggest factor, and it determines how much the other factors can contribute.
explanations.d: Incorrect. All four factors do affect transpiration, but their effects depend on the state of other factors, particularly whether stomata are open.

toLevel5.stem: In a sealed greenhouse, transpiration slows over time because the air becomes {{blank:1}} with water vapour, reducing the concentration gradient.
When stomata are closed due to darkness, changes in wind or humidity have {{blank:1}} effect on transpiration because there is little surface area for evaporation.
